 '520 drains discharge wastewater in the Yamuna': SC raps admin over rising pollution despite huge spending 
 Trending Devendra Yadav Kalyan Banerjee Deborah Bergamini PM Modi Iran War Manoj Tiwari Prince Williams Lalit Modi Giacomo Filibeck Kulgam Terrorist Encounter Devendra Yadav Kalyan Banerjee Deborah Bergamini PM Modi Iran War Manoj Tiwari Prince Williams Lalit Modi Giacomo Filibeck Kulgam Terrorist Encounter Devendra Yadav Kalyan Banerjee Deborah Bergamini PM Modi Iran War Manoj Tiwari Prince Williams Lalit Modi Giacomo Filibeck Kulgam Terrorist Encounter '520 drains discharge wastewater in the Yamuna': SC raps admin over rising pollution despite huge spending 
 Edited by Aastha Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 16, 2026, 17:26 IST Save Comments Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 Print SC says Yamuna pollution has worsened despite heavy spending and directs CPCB to monitor water quality across state and district boundaries NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Monday pulled up civic authorities and Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) over the worsening pollution in the Yamuna despite large sums being spent on cleaning the river. The bench of Justices Manoj Misra and Manmohan directed CPCB to monitor water quality where the river and 520 drains enter and exit states, Union territories and districts. It also said authorities would be held accountable if water quality deteriorates in their jurisdiction, news agency PTI reported citing an order dated November 4. The matter has been listed for further hearing on January 13. "This court is of the opinion that everything that is wrong with the civic administration in towns, cities and villages situated along the banks of the river is reflected in the poor health of the river and in the 520 drains that discharge wastewater into the Yamuna. This is why, despite huge sums being spent on cleaning the river, pollution in the Yamuna has only increased," the bench said The court said industrial pollutants and untreated sewage must be stopped at the source. It observed that building more sewage treatment plants alone would not be enough to address the problem. The bench said sewage should first be tapped and then treated wherever pollution cannot be prevented at the source. However, it flagged the difficulty of doing so because of weak sewage networks and the mixing of stormwater and sewage drains. "Where that is not possible, the sewage must first be tapped and then treated. However, tapping will remain a challenge in absence of a robust sewage system and due to joining of stormwater and sewage drains. This court is further of the opinion that it would be difficult, if not impossible, for civic authorities to tap sewage in most illegal and unauthorised colonies built on encroached land, since they have not been built on a grid layout and have hardly any space for laying a sewage system," it said. Authorities to face penalties for worsening water quality
 The Supreme Court directed the CPCB to track water quality at the entry and exit points of states, Union territories and districts. If the water deteriorates on any parameter while passing through a jurisdiction, the concerned administration will be held accountable and penalised. "If the water quality deteriorates on any parameter while flowing through, or exiting a state/Union territory or a district therein, that state/Union territory or district... shall be held accountable and penalised. The said compensation/ fine shall be deposited with the registry of this court," the bench said. The court asked the CPCB to propose a formula for calculating the compensation or fine. It also directed the board to investigate incidents indicating pollution in the river, including fish deaths, white foam on the surface, eutrophication or algal blooms, and spikes in biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD) or total suspended solids (TSS).  The CPCB's reports must identify the causes of such incidents or increases in pollution levels and recommend remedial measures, the court said. The bench further directed central and state ministries, departments and agencies to provide the CPCB and its experts with administrative, technical, logistical and operational support. Public and private entities involved in wastewater, solid waste and effluent treatment have also been asked to provide CPCB officials and designated third-party agencies unrestricted access to their premises, installations and records. This includes access for surprise inspections, sample collection, audits and checks of monitoring equipment. The court said plant operators and concerned authorities must also provide complete data access and cooperate with the integration of their systems into the CPCB's centralised monitoring network.
